jobs.prompt: Dispatch the aros subagent for a routine wake-up. Tell it: read GUARDRAILS.md and strategy.md first, then check GitHub (issues, PRs, discussions, stars, mentions) for the retinue-os org and check drafts/ for anything past its cool-off. Pick up at most one or two items, chosen to serve the strategy. Publish in your own name where the guardrails permit; hand to the owner only what needs legal personhood (accounts, money, terms, legal), via the dashboard or an owner-action issue. Write what happened to log.md and update the relevant file in projects/, and commit that record before it is complete rather than after — a run past the 900 s SCHEDULER_JOB_TIMEOUT is not stopped, only unsupervised, and the next tick may be staging the same tree, so stage named paths only and never `git add -A` (c382, c383). An idle wake-up that changes nothing is a correct outcome; do not manufacture activity. One check belongs in every survey, and it reads the **served** copy rather than the working tree, for **all five cards rather than one**: run `python3 tools/delivery-check.py`, which fetches every document under https://retinue-os.github.io/retinue-os-chamber/data/ , compares each `generated` stamp with the clock and with its disk copy, and fails if the five disagree with each other. That URL is the dashboard a reader actually opens, and the 26 h bound is a claim about the reader, not about a file on disk. Reading one card and calling it the class is the error c241 found: partial regeneration has reached the served site 4 times in 22 data commits, and it was only ever caught because `briefing.json` happened to be the stale one. If the served stamp is more than 26 hours old, attribute the failure before doing any work: read the stamp in docs/data/briefing.json too — if the disk copy is stale as well, the daily aros-dashboard-refresh job did not complete, and that wake-up's single pickup is regenerating the five data files; if the disk copy is fresh, the refresh ran and the delivery path failed, so check /pages and /pages/builds on the chamber repo instead of regenerating anything. Either miss is silent everywhere else and is recorded in log.md.

Restoring needs no argument; only slowing down does. The cost c203 cited for the fast tick (c184: the filing rate is a property of this interval) is now bounded by a separate instrument — the c184 one-issue-per-24 h rate limit — so the interval no longer sets the filing rate. Re-slow to 10800 s if 24 h pass with no human activity anywhere in the org, i.e. not before 2026-07-29T13:59:34Z. Either Aros or the owner may set it either way. See strategy.md, 'Wake cadence'. Prompt extended 2026-07-28 (cycle 223) with a dashboard staleness check: aros-dashboard-refresh failed twice (2026-07-21 on a 429 spend limit, 2026-07-23 on an API error), each time leaving the public dashboard 48 h stale with nothing anywhere recording it, and its 2026-07-28 run finished in 875 s against the 900 s timeout. This job runs 48x more often than that one, so it is the cheap place to notice. 26 h, not 24 h, so a run that merely started late does not trip it.

jobs.prompt: Dispatch the aros subagent to refresh the public project dashboard. Tell it: regenerate all five of docs/data/briefing.json, projects.json, todo.json (the owner's desk), messages.json and agenda.json — those five files and no others; the card names live in docs/index.html and docs/components/ — from the current state of projects/, log.md, and the live GitHub org data via gh. Regenerate all five together or none: one card corrected while four contradict it is worse than five that are uniformly stale. This job exists to keep the stamp inside the 26 h bound that every routine wake-up checks, so run unconditionally on every dispatch and write a fresh stamp even when nothing in the source data moved -- the mandatory delivery-check's disk-is-fresh-do-not-regenerate verdict is written for the routine aros-tick survey deciding whether an unscheduled regen is warranted, not for this job deciding whether to do the one thing it exists to do. Measured failure, 2026-08-21 (cycle 936): this job's own dispatch ran the delivery-check first out of habit, read disk as 24 h old and therefore fresh, applied the survey verdict to itself, and skipped -- leaving the same untouched stamp to cross the 26 h bound about two hours later, caught only because the next routine wake-up happened to run the same check. Keep the numbers honest — no rounding up, no invented traction. Every sentence whose truth changes with the clock names its anchor explicitly ('as of 2026-07-27 08:20 UTC, nine of the ten items are over a week old', not 'nine of the ten are now over a week old'), and an age is printed with the absolute instant it counts from ('opened 2026-07-20 11:04:39 UTC — 7 d 0 h at this stamp'), so a reader whose clock is later than the stamp can do the arithmetic instead of being misled by it. Commit and push the result. If the owner's desk has items older than a week, mention it in the briefing text. Where a card describes this page's own refresh guarantee, state what is actually enforced and nothing more: all five cards carry one measurement stamp, this job regenerates them daily, and every wake-up checks the served copies against a 26 h bound. Do not publish a promise that any wake-up finding a changed number regenerates the page — a full regeneration costs most of a 900 s job and four wake-ups on 2026-07-29 falsified that sentence within a day of its being printed. A count that has moved on since the stamp is not a false statement; a sentence that has become untrue is, and that one is corrected on sight. You are running under a 900 s SCHEDULER_JOB_TIMEOUT, and what it does is narrower than this line claimed until 2026-08-02: it does not kill you. Measured at c383, the scheduler signals only its direct child and then stops waiting, so a session past 900 s keeps running unsupervised while the next job is dispatched onto the same working tree. The failure mode is a lost *record* and a possible second session staging your files, not a clean stop. The discipline is unchanged and matters more for it: measure first, write second, have all five files committed by 600 s (push too, when the push succeeds), and stage the five named paths only — never `git add -A`, since another session may be holding the same tree. If the measurements are not finished by then, commit the five you have from one consistent stamp rather than losing the run — a complete set from a slightly narrower measurement beats nothing at all. Length budgets, and they are about what the cards render rather than about how long you take: every card puts one item on one line and none of them clip, so a paragraph in a one-line slot is a wall of text on a phone. The numbers live in tools/card-budget-check.py and nowhere else — two copies of a budget drift silently — so run `python3 tools/card-budget-check.py` before you commit and shorten whatever it reports; it prints each field's budget beside the measured max. It exits non-zero while anything is over, and reading the disk copies is only sound because the delivery check proves the served copies match them. Measured 2026-07-29 against the cards then live: 70 of 89 budgeted values over, the worst at 10.4x. Where the argument is longer than the slot, the slot carries the one-line verdict and the issue number that holds the detail ('chamber#6: no PR scope, 6 corrections waiting, oldest 8 d'), never the argument itself — the issue is the durable venue and the card is the index. The desk card is a queue, not a digest: an issue named in the previous generation must not vanish from this one without a reason. Run `python3 tools/desk-drop-check.py` before you commit; it prints every reference the last generation carried that this one does not, with its state. A closed one is the correct case. For an open one, either keep it on the card or say in the commit message why it left — at c262 seven open issues (retinue#28/#36/#37/#38/#39/#40, qlever-dir#10) left the desk in one regeneration and nothing recorded it, because the length instrument passed and no instrument asked. The same instrument now asks the reverse question, and that one costs him time rather than merely losing work: an item that stays on the desk after its subject merged or closed is an instruction to redo finished work. `desk-drop-check.py` reports those as STALE-RESOLVED and exits non-zero. On the 2026-07-31T18:35:03Z card it named two, and they are different cases: retinue#42 merged 2026-07-29T12:34:13Z, so that item was **untrue at its own stamp** and is a defect this job wrote — resolve an item's state before you list it, not after; retinue#55 merged 19:33:40Z, 58 minutes later, which is the clock moving on and is not a false statement. Drop the first kind before you commit; the second kind is what a daily cadence costs and is not yours to fix. Both questions only reach a reference the tool can resolve, so **a desk item that names an issue, a PR or a branch names its repository** — `retinue#59`, `chamber#9`, `qlever-dir#3`, never a bare `#59`; for a branch, write the repository in the same slot before the name (`chamber#7: merge or reject branch claude/…` resolves, `Branch fix/restore-dropped-merges awaits merge or deletion` does not). Branches were added to the checker at c355 and resolve the other way round — a branch is finished when `GET /repos/…/branches/<name>` returns 404, so a **gone** branch still on the desk is STALE-RESOLVED and a **live** one that left the desk is DROPPED-LIVE. On that same card 12 references were bare and went unchecked (coverage 27/36), among them `Your PRs #49, #51, #53, #56, #57 are open` — true at 18:35:03Z, all five merged between 13 and 69 minutes after it, and invisible to the checker in either direction. Write the prefix; do not let the extractor guess, which is what it was built not to do. Explicitly not a speed fix: c223 measured the durations and found output size does not explain them, and c226 re-measured that across all five files (13.0–29.1 s/KB, the largest output the second-fastest run). Do not let a shorter card be read as progress on the 900 s wall; that question is still open.
jobs.comment: 86400 s is the floor, not the schedule. The page carries a queue (the owner's desk), and a queue's freshness requirement is set by the arrival rate of the things in it — so any tick that makes a number on the page false regenerates all five files itself, and this job only guarantees a daily minimum (cycle 191). Fires at last_run + interval, read from /root/.retinue/scheduler/aros-dashboard-refresh.json; the timestamp inside docs/data/*.json is when a tick last wrote them and is not this job's schedule (cycle 192). Prompt corrected 2026-07-27 (cycle 212): it had named 'milestones' and 'community', two files that have never existed in any commit of this repo, and left agenda.json and messages.json unnamed — the five data files have carried their present names since the initial commit 63b62f4 on 2026-07-18. It now names the five that exist, points at docs/index.html as the authority for card names, and carries c210's anchor rule inline, because the rule was recorded only in projects/public-surface.md and this job is a separate cold dispatch that is not told to read it. Prompt extended again 2026-07-28 (cycle 223), same defect class as c212 and found by reading this job's *durations* rather than its text: completed runs measure 253, 323, 467, 727, 519, 566, 875 s, and the last is 97.2% of the 900 s SCHEDULER_JOB_TIMEOUT. c192's standing rule — commit before the wake-up's last third, because a kill destroys everything uncommitted — lives in a subsection of an 84 KB strategy.md. Every dispatch of the aros subagent is told to read that file (.retinue/agents/aros.md, step 2), so the rule is reachable from here; what is measurable is that nine runs never applied it and the durations grew to 97% of the wall. Now the deadline is in the prompt itself, with an explicit 600 s commit point. Output size does not explain the growth (the 2026-07-28 briefing text is 5823 chars against 7742 the day before), so nothing was trimmed on a guess; what is fixed is the part that is certain regardless of cause.

Pulls the chamber's documented manual refresh handle (docs/examples/provenance/README.md). qlever-dir's watcher fires on .nt/.ttl/.n3 changes only, so a Markdown edit never triggers a rebuild (qlever-dir#3) — this chamber holds nothing but Markdown apart from the two demo .nt files. Measured at c213 (2026-07-27 20:47Z): the store's copy of the project frontmatter was ~36 h behind disk, serving public-surface.md as of cycle 192. Rewriting this file with byte-identical content reindexed the whole chamber in 22-25 s and made all six project files current; the rewrite leaves the working tree clean, so it produces no commits and no git noise. Delete this job together with the two demo .nt files when qlever-dir#3 is fixed. Command form corrected at c214 (2026-07-27 23:5xZ): the c213 version was `cp file /tmp/x && cat /tmp/x > file`, and `>` truncates before it writes. A crash in that window left the demo file empty AND the next hourly run would have copied the empty file over the /tmp backup, destroying the only spare copy (git would still have held it, but nothing would have said so). Now: copy beside the original, then atomic same-directory rename. qlever-dir's orchestrator.py watches `close_write,create,delete,move`, so MOVED_TO on a .nt path triggers the rebuild exactly as close_write did; the .tmp suffix keeps the intermediate file from triggering one of its own. Verified end to end at c214.

jobs.prompt: Dispatch the aros subagent for the scheduled strategy review. Tell it: re-evaluate strategy.md against the evidence of the period — log.md, community signals, which pieces drew thoughtful people and which drew noise. Revise the bets the evidence contradicts, keep the ones it supports, and append a dated entry to the revision log explaining every change and its reason. A 'no change' outcome is valid but must be argued, not defaulted to. Work in committed checkpoints, because this job is heavier than a routine wake-up and runs under the same 900 s SCHEDULER_JOB_TIMEOUT: measured over 388 aros-tick runs to 2026-08-02, the median is 428 s and the p90 of the last four days is 720–857 s, with 15 runs reaching the wall. Reaching it does not stop the session — the scheduler signals its direct child and stops waiting, then dispatches the next tick onto the same working tree (c383), and that is how c382's record was lost written-but-uncommitted. So append the revision-log entry and commit it before expanding any section, commit again after each further change, and stage named paths only — never `git add -A`. Do not trust any wake-up's claim about how many inputs you have: measured at c385, the running total is an incremented adjective, not a count — the series restarted at c369 (c355 declared the twenty-eighth, c369 the fifth) and both series name this same review. strategy.md's section "The review's input count is not a count (cycle 385)" carries the full index of all 37 declarations with the cycle each came from; work from that table rather than from the last entry's number, and recompute the total with the grep it documents before stating one.
